doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

chapter: The music industry and the press
title: The young lions era and Wynton Marsalis
summary: Wilson on the origins of the young lions and musicians signed without apprenticeship.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Who started that by the way? Anybody know?

Well that point is often debated and discussed. I don’t think it was any one person. I think it was a combination of forces. Generally speaking, and I’m not going to say that Wynton Marsalis is responsible for that, he’s not. Because when Wynton came on the scene it actually was responsible for a lot of young guys like myself having an interest in the music. And seeing a guy from our generation who could play and had a great love and respect for the music certainly had an effect on many of us. So I think — and on some level he’s responsible for the way that young musicians that came through having a sense of tradition and history of the music. But on the other hand the industry, the same industry which exposed Wynton also was deciding which young musicians were going to

get a record deal, or to be able to record as a leader. So by the time the late 80s came around, early 90s, you had musicians who had never played with anybody and were getting signed to major record deals. People who had never served any apprenticeship. And that’s not the way this music has evolved. It’s always evolved by way of apprenticeships and the oral tradition, where you go and learn from the older musicians and spend time with them and go on the road with them and get knocked around and learn tunes and learn how to be a total musician. Learn how to play in the big band, learn how to play in the studio. So that — the rules changed. The rules changed drastically from like the 80s on. And now it’s going through another transition because all of this big industry stuff is now going by the wayside. Where you have people like SONY Records and Verve that dropped a lot of artists in recent months. So I think this can turn into a positive because it puts the music back into the hands of the musicians. And if we just take care of the music and take care of each other, and not put so much credence into what Down Beat magazine says or what SONY Records says or whatever agency or festival says about yeah well this is the hot young guy right now, this is who we should be listening to and who we should be booking. No. The music always determines that. It’s always about the music. It’s not about the industry, it’s about the music.
